newsitem.title: ITALY: Albanian minister says civil war averted.
newsitem.headline: Albanian minister says civil war averted.

text.p: The situation in the south of Albania is "completely out of control" but the risk of civil war has diminished, Albanian Foreign Minister Tritan Shehu was quoted as saying in an Italian newspaper published on Tuesday.

The leftist daily L'Unita reported Shehu as saying in an interview in Tirana on Monday that banks and libraries had been ransacked in Vlore and Saranda and that a navy ship had been seized also by "rebels" in the south.
However he said that a state of emergency declared by the government had calmed the situation.

"With this ruling the risk of civil war has diminished hugely. If we had not taken it, do you know what would have happened? That today Tirana would have been attacked by the rebels," he told the newspaper in the interview on Monday.
"Up to now we have tried to act as prudently as possible to avoid armed clashes and bloodbaths. This line has not paid off and now the military operations start."
Asked whether this meant that the army would now attack the south, Shehu replied:
"Nothing of the sort. We will act calmly. It will probably take a few days to reinforce the law in Vlore. In the meantime, however, the rebels must hand over their weapons."

Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta called on Tuesday for a broad and flexible government in Tirana and for continued international pressure on Albanian authorities to stop the crisis leading to a police state.

"We think the Albanian government should show flexibility," Andreatta told reporters, noting that the collapse of dubious savings schemes which sparked the crisis in Europe's poorest country had caused widespread resentment with the ruling class.
"Political management must now come through a very broad government, including the largest possible number of political parties and moral and social groups in the country," he said.

"Italy, together with other European governments is putting pressure on the Albanian government so that the state of siege does not lead to a police state, but to a resumption of democracatic life," Andreatta said.

The Albanian government, facing violent unrest in the impoverished Balkan state, has issued orders to shoot armed rioters on sight, imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew and curbed press freedoms after parliament declared a state of emergency.
The unrest erupted after thousands of people were left penniless by the collapse of pyramid investment schemes.

Dini, who was quoted in La Stampa as saying Albania urgently needed a new democratic government to restore stability, was due to address the Senate (upper house) on Wednesday on the situation in Italy's near neighbour.

Two deputies from the hard-left Communist Refoundation party urged Italy, with its European Union partners, to seek the suspension of Albania from the Council of Europe and called for international observers to be sent to the Balkan state.
The rightist Democratic party of President Sali Berisha has 122 seats in the 140-member parliament.
The Albanian government of Prime Minister Aleksander Meksi and his ministers resigned on Saturday. Opposition parties have called for the creation of a technocrat government.
On Monday, Italy sent helicopters to Vlore, to evacuate 35 people, mostly foreigners, from the riot-torn port.
